item.title: North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?
item.description:
Residents sit at a viewing platform overlooking the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters
View image in fullscreen
Residents sit at a viewing platform overlooking the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters
North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?
Kim Jong-un has opened the borders to both his key allies in Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, but for different reasons
For more than a decade, local Chinese residents pilloried it as nothing more than an empty bridge that led to a North Korean vegetable patch on the other side.
Fast forward 12 years and dozens of trucks are now traversing the bridge linking China to North Korea, boosting trade for the reclusive regime. But it has also triggered concern that it could intensify a struggle for influence over the North between Beijing and the region’s other major power, Russia.map
The New Yalu River Bridge connects the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju in North Korea and has four lanes and stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu river. It is expected to ease congestion on the ageing Friendship Bridge nearby.
It opened on 15 October, about a month after another major crossing – this time between North Korea and Russia. The first road bridge across their short shared border, named the Yakov Novichenko Bridge, reportedly made Chinese officials uneasy, coming on top of signs from the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that he is prioritising ties with Moscow.map
“China’s interest in buttressing its influence in North Korea is certainly reinforced by the diversifying North Korea-Russia relationship — ties that China tolerates but watches closely as they add complexity to its relationship with its provocative neighbour,” says Carla Freeman, director of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Foreign Policy Institute.

item.title: Severe flooding in eastern Spain and UK hit by first named storm of winter
item.description:
A firefighter pumps out water from a flooded garage in Guardamar de la Safor, Valencia, Spain. Photograph: Natxo Frances/EPA
View image in fullscreen
A firefighter pumps out water from a flooded garage in Guardamar de la Safor, Valencia, Spain. Photograph: Natxo Frances/EPAAnalysis
Severe flooding in eastern Spain and UK hit by first named storm of winter Megan Davies, Claire Jones and Magdalena Shopova for MetDesk
Storm Adam brings torrential rain to Valencia, Alicante and Balearic Islands, as Storm Austen strikes England and Wales
Storm Adam brought torrential rain to eastern Spain earlier this week. In Pego, Alicante, 632mm fell in 36 hours, with 430mm of this falling in just six hours, while the Valencian town of Olivia received 600mm in 24 hours.
The severe flooding led 145 municipalities across Valencia and Alicante to impose a temporary lockdown on about 850,000 people on Monday. At least five people have died, 500 have been rescued and 2,100 evacuated.
The storm also affected the Balearic Islands, with more than 130 incidents recorded in Ibiza including standing water at the airport causing some flights to be diverted or suspended. Although the worst of the storm has passed and conditions are improving across Valencia and Alicante, local disruption is expected to continue.
The first named storm of the winter for the UK is tracking through the Channel. Storm Austen is bringing damaging winds not only to south-west England and Wales, but south-west Ireland and northern France. Gusts are expected to be around 50-60mph, but some exposed north-western coasts of France could experience winds of up to 80-90mph.
View image in fullscreen
A car is surrounded by fallen branches in Falmouth, England, after Storm Austen made landfall. Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/Getty Images

item.title: Magnitude-7 earthquake hits Tibet, killing at least 16 and destroying hundreds of homes
item.description:
Rescuers searching through building ruins in Nagqu city after a quake hit northern Tibet. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Rescuers searching through building ruins in Nagqu city after a quake hit northern Tibet. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images
Magnitude-7 earthquake hits Tibet, killing at least 16 and destroying hundreds of homes
Search and rescue efforts under way after quake strikes region’s north, with at least seven aftershocks recorded
A magnitude-7 earthquake has hit Tibet, killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and destroying hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media have said.
Search and rescue efforts continued after at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds collapsed, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials. It was the biggest quake in the region in the past five years, according to China’s national broadcaster CCTV.
More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed to help rescue efforts. Supplies were also sent into the region, including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, about 3,000 tents, folding beds, torches and winter clothing.
The US Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10.33pm local time on Thursday, with its epicentre 119 miles (191km) east-north-east of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet. It put the earthquake’s depth at 11 miles.
The agency recorded at least seven aftershocks of magnitudes between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 6 miles. Videos posted by CCTV showed workers running out of restaurants and objects falling off shelves at supermarkets when the quake struck.
Moment magnitude-7 earthquake strikes China’s Tibet
China’s official Xinhua news agency said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities had taken emergency actions to stop trains passing through the region.

item.title: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes
item.description:
Huang Yi-hao was left with a bruised pelvis after the men rammed him with a car while he was riding his scooter. Photograph: Huang Yi-hao/Facebook
View image in fullscreen
Huang Yi-hao was left with a bruised pelvis after the men rammed him with a car while he was riding his scooter. Photograph: Huang Yi-hao/Facebook
Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes
Person named ‘K’ from China paid five defendants to injure Huang Yi-hao, New Taipei prosecutors say
Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party and Xi Jinping.
Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression to silence critics on the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory and has vowed to take by force if necessary.
In one performance, Huang Yi-hao insulted the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie-the-Pooh and tore into his political record.
Prosecutors in New Taipei said on Wednesday that an individual from mainland China who was identified as “K” had paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalisation.
The prosecutors said: “This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence.”
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment.
A GPS tracker was allegedly put on Huang’s scooter months before the attack to identify his daily routines, Taiwan’s Central News Agency said. On 11 September, two defendants drove into Huang’s bike as he rode home, but stopped after hearing Huang scream, prosecutors said.
The comedian was left with a bruised pelvis and the suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim in order to send a photo of Huang’s medical certificate to K.

item.title: US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies
item.description:
The smartphone app DeepSeek. Photograph: Andy Wong/AP
View image in fullscreen
The smartphone app DeepSeek. Photograph: Andy Wong/AP
US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies
Use of tools ‘may result in the transfer of sensitive data’ to China, defense department says
The US government on Monday ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence (AI) tools from the Chinese startup DeepSeek, as the countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector.
A notice from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek – and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties – saying they must be removed from IT devices.
The DHS can issue direction to civilian agencies but not the military or intelligence services. The US defense department did not respond to an AFP request for comment.
“DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” said a document attached to Monday’s notice.
Use of DeepSeek AI tools “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to [China] if used by US government employees or vendors”, the department warned.
Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government “extensive authority” to access private company infrastructure, it said.
DeepSeek has been contacted for comment.
One of China’s top AI labs, DeepSeek shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance.
The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and earlier in October updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4.
The US has accused DeepSeek and other top Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing the capabilities of cutting-edge models developed by American rivals.
Despite their fierce competition in the field, when their leaders Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met at the White House in September, China and the US agreed to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents.

item.title: The Guardian view on Trump and Putin: Ukraine’s future is not theirs to bargain away | Editorial
item.description:
‘Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments.’ Photograph: José Luis Magaña/AP
View image in fullscreen
‘Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments.’ Photograph: José Luis Magaña/AP
The Guardian view on Trump and Putin: Ukraine’s future is not theirs to bargain away Editorial
Russia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strong
Does Vladimir Putin know exactly how to play Donald Trump? The history of chummy phone calls, high-profile meetings and attempts to bring Russia in from the cold certainly suggests that Moscow’s thuggish ruler has a hold on this American president. If Mr Trump agrees to negotiate Ukraine’s future with Mr Putin and China’s Xi Jinping without Ukraine at the table, he will have handed the Russian leader a victory before talks begin. The message will be that strongmen are ruling the world and determining the fate of weaker nations.
Ukraine has the right to determine its future. That right cannot be waved away by a self-serving Russian proposal, however much it indulges Mr Trump’s belief that world affairs should be settled by powerful men. The scales are falling from European eyes. Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments. If Washington now rewards Moscow and pressures Ukraine to accept a raw deal, it would be a betrayal. European governments would wonder where America might be in the future when their own security is threatened.

item.title: China’s economy grows faster than forecast after AI boom boosts exports
item.description:
China’s economy has grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year. Photograph: Peter Parks/AFP/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
China’s economy has grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year. Photograph: Peter Parks/AFP/Getty Images
China’s economy grows faster than forecast after AI boom boosts exports
Third-quarter GDP up by 4.5% compared with last year as industrial output is buoyed by electronics demand
Roaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending.
China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%.
China’s economy has now grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, putting it on track to hit the government’s 2026 target of 4.5%-5% growth without extra stimulus measures.
Industrial production rose 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August, while retail sales only increased 1.1%, up from 0.4%.
Duncan Wrigley, the chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said Beijing’s policymakers were likely to conclude that their efforts to stabilise headline growth in the third quarter were successful.
“Headline industrial production rose in September partly as coalmines resumed operations after safety inspections prompted by a major accident. Manufacturing output growth remained robust at 6.0% year on year in September, buoyed up by stronger export demand for electronics, AI-related equipment and autos,” Wrigley said.
“Hi-tech manufacturing output continues to outperform traditional sectors, as China climbs the value-added ladder,” Wrigley added.
However, fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% over the first nine months, property investment tumbled by 20.6%, and infrastructure spending remained weak.

item.title: The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information | Editorial
item.description:
The exterior of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Photograph: Smirnov Vladimir/Anadolu/Getty
View image in fullscreen
The exterior of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Photograph: Smirnov Vladimir/Anadolu/Getty
The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information Editorial
In the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemics
Is there a plague outbreak in Russia? If the answer were a clear yes, there shouldn’t be much reason to worry. With swift medical intervention, plague is treatable. But in the nearly three weeks since a worker at a Siberian plague research unit died of a mysterious respiratory illness, state officials have been consistently tight-lipped about what happened and whether there were any further cases.
It is this uncertainty that has the World Health Organization (WHO) and international community worried: partly because there is a – very small – risk of an outbreak, and partly because it is yet another warning that the international coordination we rely on to prevent pandemics is fraying along with the rest of international politics, and could easily fail to protect us in the future.
The key to containing an outbreak is quick disclosure and open sharing of information. Russia reportedly held high-level meetings about the case, quarantined the hospital where the worker was treated and traced about 200 contacts. That response suggests officials believed the infection was plague, and yet they did not report any of this to the WHO, as international law requires. Russia later revealed that the worker died of a pneumonia of unknown origin – hardly useful information. It undoubtedly gathered lab results and genetic sequences that could shed more light on the case, but has not shared them.

item.title: China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
item.description:
The concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragedies

When Leon Lv was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods.

“I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-west China. “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.”

item.title: Like dinosaur eggs in the sand: the pterosaur museum built to thrive in the Gobi desert
item.description:
How architects worked with harsh environment to create sustainable building in location where fossils were found

Viewed from afar, the silver-hued Hami Pterosaur Museum almost looks like a space base on Mars. Viewed from above, it resembles a collection of dinosaur eggs in the sand. Nestled in the Gobi desert, in north-west China, the new tourist attraction showcases hundreds of impressive fossils of pterosaurs, ancient flying reptiles related to dinosaurs. But far from reflecting its prehistoric exhibits, the building itself is a modern-day architectural specimen.

Designed with underground exhibition halls, giant light funnels and sprawling solar farms, the museum is able to operate sustainably while withstanding an extremely harsh environment.
